blocks.title: Close the openings you never chose
blocks.body: Your router may hold inbound openings nobody picked on purpose: a mapping an app asked for, a forward from a project long finished, remote administration left on. Today you audit them on your own router, close the silent ones, and prove they stay closed.

blocks.heading: What you bring to the audit

items.label: Your listener inventory
items.detail: Each LAN-facing listener from part 4 is something an opening could reach.

items.label: Your dated baseline
items.detail: Every change you make today gets recorded there, like part 5 taught.

items.label: Translation is not permission
items.detail: From part 6: a missing mapping is not a stated rule, so openings are checked by name, not assumed.

items.label: Admin access to your own router
items.detail: Your router, your credentials, or the explicit okay of the person whose router it is.

blocks.heading: One worked audit, start to finish
rows: Close. Last summer's game server, nobody hosts now. A stale UPnP mapping is exposure nobody chose.
Keep. Matches the household NAS remote access the owner set up and still uses. Named, with a reason.
Unknown → then kept. Not in anyone's records; the owner identified it as the NAS admin fallback and chose to keep it. Unknown stays open until named.
Remote administration from the internet: off
Nothing to close. Off is the default worth keeping; record that it was checked.
blocks.caption: An invented example household. Your router will show different entries; the verdicts come from your records, not from this table.

blocks.heading: How each verdict was reached
blocks.body: No entry was judged by its name alone. The Terraria mapping was closed because the household's own records showed a finished project, not because games are suspicious. The 443 mapping was kept because the owner named it and gave a current reason. The 8443 forward started as unknown: it matched nothing in anyone's notes, so the next step was asking the authorized owner, who identified it. Until a finding is named, it stays unknown — unknown is not closed by guessing, and it is not kept by default either. If the owner had not recognized 8443, the verdict would have been close, with the change recorded so it could be restored by name if something broke.

blocks.heading: Run the audit on your own router
items: Sign in to your router's admin page with your own credentials, or get the explicit okay of the person whose router it is.
Find the UPnP setting and the list of active mappings. Write down the state and every mapping.
Find the port-forwarding list (sometimes called virtual servers). Write down every forward.
Find remote administration or WAN management. Write down whether it is on.
Label each entry keep, close or unknown, using your own records first and the authorized owner for anything unfamiliar.
Close the silent entries one change at a time: delete stale forwards and mappings, and turn UPnP off if nothing you are keeping needs it.
Record every change in your dated baseline before you test anything.

columns.name: Inside: the router's own lists
columns.detail: After your changes, the closed entry no longer appears in the UPnP or forwarding lists, and the router still shows the keeps you named. A reboot later, the lists still match your baseline.

columns.name: Outside: an attempt you own
columns.detail: From your own phone on cellular — not Wi-Fi, so you are genuinely outside — try the closed address and port. It fails. One side alone is not proof: the list could hide a mapping, and a failed attempt could be a wrong address. Together they close the question.

blocks.heading: The port fails from outside. What is the listener doing?
blocks.prompt: You deleted the stale forward and proved the port fails from your phone on cellular. Back inside, the NAS still listens on 0.0.0.0:8443. What do you know?
options: The service is off, because the outside attempt failed
The boundary no longer passes that port from outside, while the listener may still serve the house — translation and permission are separate
The router is broken, because the listener is still running
blocks.explanation: A closed opening is about the boundary, not the process. The listener on your LAN can keep serving the house; what changed is that no mapping or rule carries a new inbound flow to it. That is part 6's distinction applied to your own audit.

blocks.title: Your router, your records, your call
blocks.body: Audit only a router you own or are explicitly authorized to change. The fill-in fields reset when you leave; keep findings in your private baseline, never posted. If closing something breaks an app — a game, a console, a camera — your record lets you re-add that one opening by name. A chosen opening with a reason is fine; silent ones are the problem. Never test addresses that are not yours.
